problem: Deep RL from raw pixels needs massive amounts of data and generalizes poorly to unseen environments; learning-from-scratch policies effectively memorize the training building and often perform no better than a blind agent at test time.
motivation: Perceptual priors about the world (3D structure, semantics) are valid assumptions that could reduce sample complexity and improve generalization for visuomotor policies. The paper asks whether standard offline mid-level vision features, used as frozen state input to RL, help, and whether one feature suffices for all tasks.
key_idea: Feed a frozen set of pretrained mid-level vision encoders (Taskonomy) as the state for RL policies instead of raw pixels, and pick a compact task-agnostic feature subset via a max-coverage (delta-cover) solver over task-taxonomy distances.
insight: Feature-based agents learn faster and generalize to unseen buildings where scratch, which overfits and is roughly as good as blind at test time, fails. No single feature is universal: rank reversal shows depth features are best for exploration and object-classification features for navigation (significant at alpha=0.0005), with a semantic/geometric split. A 4-feature max-coverage set nearly matches or exceeds the best task-specific feature without a noticeable loss in sample efficiency. In VizDoom, the advantage disappeared once training textures were randomized to resemble test textures, so the gain comes from reducing the train/test shift.
method: Frozen mid-level encoders: 20 Taskonomy ResNet-50 encoders (without global average pooling, 16x16 spatial features), trained offline on 4M indoor images; only the policy is trained.

RL training: PPO with GAE, made off-policy with an ACER-like replay buffer and importance reweighting because Gibson rendering allows only one rollout worker; hyperparameters tuned for the scratch baseline and reused for all features.
Hypothesis testing protocol: 3-8 seeds per condition, Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control (Q=20%), and rank-reversal tests across tasks.

Max-Coverage Feature Selector: uses Taskonomy task-affinity distances to find a size-k subset that is a delta-cover of all features with minimal delta, via binary search over Boolean integer programs (under 5 s).
Calibrated metric: reward relative to blind, RR_blind = (r_treatment - r_min)/(r_blind - r_min).

Control baselines: scratch (AtariNet on RGB), blind, random frozen projection, downsampled pixels as features, random actions, and SOTA feature learning (forward/inverse dynamics, curiosity, DARLA, ImageNet pretraining, AE/VAE).
Tasks: visual-target navigation (find crate, sparse reward), visual exploration (occupancy cell reveal), local planning (coordinate goal); actions are turn_left, turn_right, move_forward.

setting.backbone: Frozen Taskonomy ResNet-50 encoders + small policy network trained with PPO (off-policy variant); scratch baseline uses AtariNet
setting.training_data: Encoders pretrained on Taskonomy (4M indoor images); policies trained by RL in a single Gibson training building (40.2 m^2 for navigation, 154.9 m^2 for exploration/local planning); ~800 policies total
setting.observation: Monocular RGB image plus minimal task-specific side information (e.g. goal coordinates), no proprioception

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (reward curves, bar charts, relative-to-blind rewards) and not in tables; no navigation benchmark metrics (SR/SPL) are reported.
results: Several mid-level feature agents significantly outperform scratch in unseen test buildings on all three tasks (p<0.002 per task), and a 4-feature max-coverage set nearly matches or exceeds the best task-specific feature. The best features beat SOTA representation learning methods (curiosity, DARLA, dynamics models, ImageNet) by a large margin. The paper claims at least an order of magnitude less data than scratch. Findings held across 9 other buildings (Spearman rho 0.93 for navigation, 0.85 for exploration) and in VizDoom.
limitations: Tasks are locomotion-only in simulation; conclusions may not transfer to manipulation, and no real-robot evaluation is reported
Fixed frozen feature set and RL-only, neural-network-only study; the approach is empirical, without guarantees on test performance
The advantage vanishes when training data is made diverse enough (texture randomization), so the benefit is specific to limited-data regimes
